ABSTRACT
The design of efficient and cost-effective bifunctional catalysts, which are capable of driving both the hydrogen evolution
reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER), is of paramount importance for advancing overall water splitting. Here,
we developed an innovative heterogeneous interface engineering strategy to boost the electrocatalytic performance of overall
water splitting. This approach involves the synergistic integration of ultra-fine CoMoP nanocrystals coupled with three-
dimensional (3D) porous C 3 N 4 /N-doped carbon (NC) architectures, constructing a distinctive CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC heteroge-
neous interface. The CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC exhibits distinguished overall water splitting performance. To drive the overall water
splitting current of 10 mA cm -2 , the CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC||CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC electrolysis cell only needs an ultralow cell voltage
of 1.496 V. The electronic properties and localized coordination environments characterizations, and density functional
theory (DFT) calculations elucidate that the improved catalytic activities of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC are primarily attributed to the
synergistic interfacial coupling between CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC heterogeneous interface. A novel multi-site synergistic catalytic
mechanism was revealed by the DFT calculations, in which the optimum H* adsorption site on CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC for HER is
on the cobalt atoms in CoMoP with the ultralow Gibbs free energy of hydrogen bonding (ΔG H* ) of 0.018 eV, while for the
OER, the optimum intermediates adsorption site of the CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC is on the carbon atoms in C 3 N 4 /NC. Besides, the
intricately engineered 3D hierarchical porous framework of the CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC can facilitate the ion and electron transport
and improve mass transfer, which gives rise to enhanced water splitting performance.
1 | Introduction
Hydrogen (H₂), with its exceptional gravimetric energy density
and zero-emission nature, has emerged as a promising sus-
tainable energy candidate [1-3]. In recent decades, due to the
high-purity hydrogen/oxygen yield and zero-pollution char-
acteristics, electrochemical water splitting, driven by renewable
energy sources (solar energy, wind energy, tidal energy, etc.),
has emerged as a focal point of global scientific research [4-6].
However, electrochemical water splitting requires efficient

electrocatalysts on both the cathode (hydrogen evolution
reaction, HER) and anode (oxygen evolution reaction, OER) for
efficient H 2 generation [7-9]. To date, platinum (Pt)-based
materials remain the benchmark electrocatalysts for the HER
[10, 11], while iridium (Ir)-and ruthenium (Ru)-based catalysts
demonstrate superior performance as state-of-the-art catalysts
for the OER [12, 13]. However, the extremely low abundance
and high cost of these precious metals hinder their commercial
applications. Besides, to enable H 2 sustainably, the development
of bifunctional catalysts, which demonstrate the ability to
concurrently catalyze both the HER and OER, could signifi-
cantly simplify electrolyzer design and reduce operational costs
[14]. Consequently, significant research efforts have been
devoted to developing non-noble metal bifunctional electro-
catalysts toward overall water-splitting, such as transitional
metal oxide [15], transition metal chalcogenides [16], layered
double hydroxides (LDHs) [17], transition metal phosphides
(TMPs) [18], transition metal nitrides [19], metal-free carbon-
based materials [20], and so on. Among these non-noble metal
bifunctional electrocatalysts, TMPs have emerged as highly
promising catalytic materials owing to their synergistic combi-
nation of exceptional catalytic activity, superior chemical sta-
bility, and remarkable electrical conductivity [21]. However, the
intrinsic HER/OER activities of TMPs still lag significantly
behind those of benchmark Pt/C and Ir/Ru. The overall water-
splitting performance and electrochemical stability of TMPs still
face critical challenges for practical applications. Hence, sub-
stantial improvements in both the electrochemical efficacy and
structural durability of TMPs remain essential to fulfill their
potential in practical applications.
Heterostructure interface engineering has been regarded as one
of the most effective strategies to enhance the catalytic activity
of the electrocatalyst; the strong interfacial coupling between
heterogeneous components in such structures enables precise
modulation of their electronic configuration, increases the
amount of accessible active sites, and induces effective syner-
gistic effects [21-24]. Furthermore, beyond serving as an
effective strategy for regulating electron redistribution, hetero-
geneous interface engineering also provides more transmission
channels for electrons, electrolytes, and gaseous products; it
improves the structural stability of the catalyst [25-27]. Mu
et al. successfully developed a bifunctional NiSe₂-Ni₂P hetero-
structure supported on a nickel foam substrate (denoted as
NiSe₂-Ni₂P/NF), demonstrating a significantly larger electro-
chemical active surface area (ECSA) and superior ECSA-
normalized catalytic performance for both HER and OER
compared to the individual NiSe₂/NF and Ni₂P/NF counter-
parts, which is attributed to three synergistic factors: improved
water adsorption kinetics, optimized hydrogen binding energy,
and strong electronic interactions between the NiSe 2 and
Ni 2 P components [28]. Ding et al. successfully synthesized
a hierarchical Co(OH) 2 /Ag/FeP heterostructure by interface
engineering strategy, which delivers a higher density of
catalytically active sites [29]. The authors revealed that
the substantial charge redistribution, occurring at the con-
structed interfaces in the Co(OH)₂/Ag/FeP heterostruc-
ture, facilitates the generation of low-charge state Fe²⁺
species and highly oxidized Co³⁺/Co⁴⁺. This electronic
modulation is identified as the key factor responsible for
the enhanced electrocatalytic performance in water-splitting
reactions. There are some other similar TMP-based hetero-
structures that have been reported for enhanced overall water
splitting performances, such as FeNi-LDH/CoP/CC [30],
V p -Co-MoP@MXene [31], CoP/Fe-Co 9 S 8 [32], Ni 2 P/NiFe-LDH
[33], and Mo─Ni 2 P/Fe x P-V/NFF [26].
Two dimensional (2D) graphitic carbon nitride (g-C 3 N 4 )
nanosheets have emerged as promising bifunctional catalysts for
both HER and OER, attributed to their distinctive physico-
chemical properties, which include tunable energy band
positions, an optimal bandgap, exceptional structural stability
under harsh electrochemical conditions, high nitrogen content,
and remarkable morphological diversity ranging from ultrathin
lamellar structures to porous architectures [34, 35]. Nevertheless,
the practical implementation of the g-C 3 N 4 is constrained by
insufficient active site density and excessively high sheet resistance
[36]. The incorporation of carbon or heteroatom-doped carbon
architectures (such as graphene [36], N-doped graphene
(N-graphene) [34], and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [37]) into
g-C 3 N 4 matrices has been demonstrated as an effective approach
to simultaneously enhance active site accessibility and optimize
electrical conductivity, thereby facilitating efficient electron
transfer kinetics [38]. When the g-C 3 N 4 coupled with transition
metals to form a heterostructure interface, the nitrogen atoms in
g-C 3 N 4 can effectively tune the electron configuration of adjacent
metal atoms through lone pair electron sharing, coupled with the
intrinsically abundant delocalized electrons in nitrogen centers of
g-C 3 N 4 , synergistically enhances the adsorption capacity of
reaction intermediates at the catalytically active metal sites [39,
40]. Besides, the complexation of TMPs with g-C 3 N 4 is an effective
approach to optimizing the catalytic activity. Zhang et al. have
engineered a novel FeNi phosphide/C 3 N 4 interfacial hetero-
structure (FeNi-C 3 N 4 -P), which can precisely modulate the
valence electronic configurations of Ni and Fe [41]. The highly
electronegative nitrogen atoms in C 3 N 4 are hypothesized to facil-
itate electron extraction from adjacent metal atoms, thereby en-
hancing the adsorption of OER intermediates at nickel active sites
through electronic modulation, and these nitrogen centers appear
to engage in coordination bonding with iron atoms by sharing
their lone pair electrons, which serves to moderate the adsorption
strength of oxygen-containing intermediates on iron sites. Zeng
et al. reported the iron phosphide/porous graphitic carbon nitride
interfacial heterostructure (FeP/g-C 3 N 4 ), in which the electrical
conductivity and charge transport are significantly enhanced,
leading to excellent catalytic activity for HER [42]. Li et al. dem-
onstrated that the remarkable H 2 evolution activity of the three
dimensional (3D)/2D NiCoP/g-C 3 N 4 heterostructure stems prin-
cipally from the synergistic Co-N and Ni-N dual bonding config-
urations established between the NiCoP nanoclusters and g-C 3 N 4
nanosheets, which remarkably enhance charge carrier migration/
separation efficiency while simultaneously strengthening hetero-
interface interaction [43]. However, current research studies on
TMPs/g-C 3 N 4 heterostructures have predominantly focused on
their applications in photocatalytic H 2 production, and the elec-
trocatalytic H 2 production performance and the catalytic mecha-
nism of TMPs/g-C 3 N 4 heterostructures have not been
systematically studied.
In this study, a novel ultra-fine bimetallic phosphide (CoMoP)
nanocrystals coupled with 3D porous C 3 N 4 /N-doped carbon
architecture (CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC) was prepared by a simple

the intrinsic chemical and electronic coupling effect between
CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC heterogeneous interface, which gives rise to
the synergistic effects.
2 | Results and Discussion
2.1 | Morphology and Structure
Supporting Information S1: Figure S1 demonstrates the X-ray
diffraction (XRD) patterns of CoMoP/C and CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC.
The diffraction peaks are well-fitted with the orthorhombic
CoMoP, indexed by the pink perpendicular lines (PDF#32-
0299), indicating the formation of CoMoP. The XRD pattern of
the C 3 N 4 /NC (Supporting Information S1: Figure S1) exhibits
well-defined characteristic peaks of C 3 N 4 , which are denoted by
vertical red reference lines (PDF#87-1526) [44]. Besides, the
simultaneous pyrolysis of C 2 H 4 N 4 (DCDA) and D314 resin
gives rise to the formation of NC, hence marking the product as
C 3 N 4 /NC. The characteristic peaks of C 3 N 4 almost disappear in
CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC, which might be attributed to the low relative
crystallinity of C 3 N 4 and unique dispersion of C 3 N 4 on the
CoMoP nanoparticles due to the efficient interaction between
the precursors and CoMoP [45, 46]. The neutron powder
diffraction (NPD) was used to investigate the crystal structure
of the CoMoP/C and CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC, as shown in Supporting
Information S1: Figure S2. After Rietveld refinements,
the volume of the unit cell (V) of CoMoP in CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC
is 144.94(1) Å 3 , with dimensions a = 5.8180(4) Å, b = 3.6912(3)
Å, c = 6.7489(5) Å, which are little bit smaller than those of
CoMoP/C (V = 145.57(2) Å 3 , a = 5.8185(5) Å, b = 3.7032(4) Å,
c = 6.7557(5) Å), suggesting the lattice contraction of CoMoP
after coupling with C 3 N 4 /NC. The lattice contraction mainly
results from the strong interaction between CoMoP and
C 3 N 4 /NC, which is consistent with the XRD results.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) characterization demon-
strates that both CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC and C 3 N 4 /NC exhibit 3D
hierarchical porous architectures formed from the assembly of
2D graphene-like carbon nanosheets (Figure 1A-C and Sup-
porting Information S1: Figure S3A,B). The unique structural
configuration effectively shortens ion transport pathways while
enhancing mass transfer efficiency through its interconnected
porous framework [47]. The SEM images of CoMoP/C
(Supporting Information S1: Figure S4A,B) reveal a granular
morphology composed of particles ranging in diameter
from a few hundred nanometers to several micrometers. The
above findings reveal that the DCDA plays the crucial
role in the formation of the 3D hierarchical porous structure.
The porous structure of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC was evaluated
through low-temperature (77 K) nitrogen adsorption-desorption
isotherm analysis using the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET)
method (Supporting Information S1: Figure S5A). The
CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC exhibits hybrid type II/IV adsorption char-
acteristics, demonstrating a BET specific surface area of
218 m² g⁻¹. Supporting Information S1: Figure S5B depicts the
pore-size distribution curve of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC, including
micropores, mesopores, and macropores. The transmission
electron microscope (TEM) images of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC
(Figure 1D,E) show that the ultra-fine CoMoP nanocrystals are
dispersed on the C 3 N 4 /NC uniformly. Notably, the mean grain
size of the CoMoP is ~3 nm (see the inset of size-distribution
histogram in Figure 1E). The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM)
images of CoMoP nanocrystal show the lattice fringes of 0.267
and 0.210 nm, which are ascribed to the (201) and (103) facets
(Figure 1F,G), and the inset in Figure 1G is the corresponding
fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern. The scanning TEM
(STEM) image of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC shows that ultra-fine Co-
MoP nanocrystals are anchored on the porous C 3 N 4 /NC
(Figure 1H). Figure 1I-N shows the elemental mapping images
of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC, which was collected from the red dashed
box in Figure 1H. Supporting Information S1: Figure S3C,D
shows the TEM images of C 3 N 4 /NC, which also reveal a similar
structure, and the lattice fringe of 0.337 nm is ascribed to the
C 3 N 4 (002). The TEM images of CoMoP/C (Supporting Infor-
mation S1: Figure S4C,D) reveal that the CoMoP nanocrystals
are dispersed on the carbon uniformly. In conclusion, the
simultaneous pyrolysis of DCDA and Co/Mo/P coupled D314
resin gives rise to the formation of the unique CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC
heterogeneous interface and the 3D hierarchical porous
structure.
2.2 | Electrical Properties
The electronic properties and localized coordination environ-
ments of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC were determined by using X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and synchrotron-based X-ray
absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy. Figure 2A
presents the X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES)
spectroscopies of CoMoP/C and CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC, with stan-
dard Mo foil and MoO 3 as references. The pre-edge region of
CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC exhibits a positive energy shift compared to
CoMoP/C, as evidenced in Figure 2B. This distinct spectral
displacement suggests enhanced interfacial electron coupling
between the CoMoP and the C 3 N 4 /NC heterostructure, likely
arising from orbital hybridization at the heterojunction inter-
face between CoMoP and C 3 N 4 /NC. The k 3 -weighted Mo
K-edge extended XAFS (EXAFS) spectroscopies of CoMoP/C
and CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC show similar oscillation, which indicates
a similar crystal structure (Figure 2C). Figure 2D shows the
corresponding Fourier transform of k 3 -weighted Mo K-edge
EXAFS and the first-shell fit curves. The broad main peak of
CoMoP/C and CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC at 2.30 Å is ascribed to the
P-Mo and Co-Mo vectors. The shoulder peak at 1.68 Å of
the CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC mainly results from the incorporation of
the N element (Mo-N bond) [48]. Supporting Information S1:
Table S1 shows the detailed fit parameters. The coordination
number (CN) of Mo-N is about 1.3, with the Mo-N distance of
2.21 Å. The P-Mo and Co-Mo CNs of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC are 5.1
and 3.1, respectively, which are a little smaller than those of
CoMoP/C (6.1 and 4.3). The Mo-P distance of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC

2.3 | HER Performances
Figure 3A demonstrates the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV)
curves of the catalysts. The overpotential at the current density
of 10 mA cm -2 (η 10 ) of C 3 N 4 /NC is 226 mV. The CoMoP/C ex-
hibits good HER activity with a small η 10 of 87 mV, which is
lower than C 3 N 4 /NC. Compared to CoMoP/C, the HER activity
of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC is highly improved with the smaller η 10 of
52 mV. The η 10 (52 mV) and η 20 (70 mV) of CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC
are very close to Pt/C (η 10 = 37 mV and η 20 = 49 mV). The
Tafel plots extracted from LSV could lead to lower Tafel
slopes and distort the actual performance [58]. To ensure

which the rapid proton discharge process is succeeded by a rate-
determining electrochemical recombination step involving
a second proton [60]. The CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC exhibits a smaller
Tafel slope than CoMoP/C (89 mV dec -1 ), indicating faster
reaction kinetics. Besides, the CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC exhibits an
exchange current density (j 0 ) of 0.487 mA cm -2 , which is much
higher than that of CoMoP/C (0.028 mA cm -2 ), indicating faster

reaction is the rate-determining step. Electrochemical imped-

between 100 KHz and 100 mHz at overpotentials of 105 mV

CN/NG [68]. Supporting Information S1: Table S2 demonstrates
the comparisons of HER performance of the nonprecious metal
catalysts in previous pieces of literature.

2.4 | OER Performances
Subsequently, the catalytic activities of the catalysts toward
OER were studied in 1.0 M KOH; the benchmark RuO 2 /C

3 | Conclusion
In summary, a bimetallic TMPs (CoMoP) coupled with 3D porous
C 3 N 4 /N-doped carbon (CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC) was successfully syn-
thesized via a simple and low-cost synthesis method. The ultra-
fine CoMoP nanocrystals are uniformly anchored on the porous
C 3 N 4 /N-doped carbon, resulting in the unique CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC
heterogeneous interface. The CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC demonstrates
exceptional bifunctional catalytic activities for both HER and
OER. CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC||CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC electrode exhibits a
very low cell voltage of 1.496 V to drive the overall water splitting
current density of 10 mA cm -2 , which outperforms the bench-
mark precious metal catalysts Pt/C||RuO 2 /C and most of the
nonprecious metal bifunctional catalysts in previous pieces of
literature. The DFT calculations reveal the unique electronic
state distribution and interfacial effects of the CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC
heterostructure, which leads to enhanced overall water splitting
performance. Besides, the unique 3D porous structure of
CoMoP/C 3 N 4 /NC establishes efficient transport pathways that
synergistically facilitate the ion and electron transport and
improve mass transfer. Overall, this study designs a unique
TMPs-based bifunctional electrocatalyst by heterogeneous inter-
face engineering and reveals a novel multi-site synergistic
catalytic mechanism. This study provides a novel perspective on
the rational design and synthesis of bifunctional electrocatalysts
for HER and OER, thereby advancing the development
of efficient water-splitting systems for sustainable hydrogen
production.
